Malignity
ma-LIG-ni-tee
n. (settled ill-will; a disposition to put the worst construction on everything)
From Latin malignitas, ill-nature, from malus, bad. The Greek word means a bad disposition, the habit of taking things in the worst sense. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's catalogue of the fruits of a mind given over.

Biblical Definition

Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers. The list belongs to the argument of Romans 1, and the structure around it matters more than any single item. Three times Paul says that God gave them up or gave them over — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and finally: even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient. The catalogue that follows is what a mind looks like when God has withdrawn his restraint, and malignity sits in it between deceit and whispering, in the company of the quieter sins. The paragraph ends at the worst point: who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them. And then, without a chapter break in the argument, Paul turns on the reader who has been agreeing: Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): extreme enmity or evil dispositions of heart towards another; malice; a disposition to put the worst construction on words and actions.

expand to see more

MALIGNITY, n. Extreme enmity, or evil dispositions of heart towards another; malice; extreme malevolence.

MALIGNITY, n. Evilness of nature; as the malignity of fraud.

WHISPERER, n. One who whispers; a tale-bearer; a secret slanderer.

REPROBATE, a. Not enduring proof or trial; abandoned in sin; lost to virtue or grace.

CENSORIOUS, a. Addicted to censure; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:29 — "Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,"

Rom 1:28 — "And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;"

Rom 1:32 — "Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them."

Rom 2:1 — "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things."

Modern Corruption

Romans 1 is read as a list of other people's sins, which is the precise use Paul anticipates and demolishes in the sentence immediately following it.

expand to see more

The chapter division here has done real damage, because Paul's argument does not pause. He builds a catalogue that any moral reader will applaud — and then turns: therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest. The list was a trap for the self-righteous, and the quieter sins in it are the teeth. Envy, debate, deceit, malignity, whispering, backbiting, boasting, disobedience to parents, covenantbreaking, unmercifulness — these are respectable-church sins, and they are in the same sentence as murder. A man who reads Romans 1 and thinks only of the culture has read it exactly as Paul feared.

Malignity itself deserves naming for what it is: not an outburst but a settled bent, the habit of assuming the worst about a person's motive and construing every ambiguous act against him. It is the opposite of the charity of 1 Corinthians 13, which thinketh no evil and believeth all things. It thrives in congregations because it never has to be confessed — it looks like discernment from the inside. The remedy is the one Romans supplies three chapters later: there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, which is a fact a malignant heart cannot hold and stay malignant.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kakoetheia (G2550), malignity, bad character, the habit of putting the worst construction on things; adokimos (G96), reprobate, rejected after testing; psithuristes (G5588), a whisperer.

expand to see more

Greek kakoetheia (G2550) — bad disposition, malignity; the one occurrence, Romans 1:29.

Greek adokimos (G96) — failing the test, rejected, reprobate; God gave them over to a reprobate mind.

Greek psithuristes (G5588) — a whisperer, a secret slanderer; next in the list.

Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to hand over, to deliver up; God gave them over.

Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse, inexcusable; thou art inexcusable, O man.

Usage

"“deceit, malignity; whisperers” — the single occurrence, among the quieter sins."

"“God gave them over to a reprobate mind” — the judgment the list illustrates."

"“Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest” — the turn."
